hints: Look carefully at label B. It points to the dark, tight single ring of small cells that separates the outer cortex from the central stele.
Remember which root layer has waterproof suberin in its walls (the Casparian strip) that forces water out of the cell walls and into the cells.
walkthrough:
**Orientate yourself in the root section**

Look from outside to inside. Label A is the large, loosely packed cortex parenchyma. The centre with big open vessels is the vascular stele. Label B is the boundary ring between them.

That boundary ring is the endodermis.

**Recall the apoplast pathway**

The apoplastic pathway is water moving through cell walls and intercellular spaces, without crossing a cell surface membrane. It is free and fast through the cortex.

It can only continue until it hits a waterproof barrier.

**Spot the barrier**

The endodermal cells have the Casparian strip, a band of waterproof suberin in their radial and transverse walls. This seals the apoplast.

Water is forced to cross the cell surface membrane into the cytoplasm and continue by the symplastic pathway. So tissue B inhibits the apoplastic path.

options.A: This is cortex parenchyma. Its thin cellulose walls and air spaces allow free apoplastic movement, so it does not block water.
options.B: This is the endodermis. Its Casparian strip of suberin is waterproof and blocks the apoplastic pathway, forcing water into the symplast.
options.C: This is phloem tissue inside the stele. It is involved in translocation of sugars, not in blocking apoplastic water entry.
options.D: This is xylem tissue (large vessels). It actually carries water upward once it has entered the stele, so it does not inhibit the pathway.
